stages.title: Human anatomy
stages.hook: An adult skeleton has over 200 bones, yet a baby is born with more. Where do the extra bones go?
explain: Anatomy is the study of the structure of the body: what parts there are, where they are and how they fit together. Doctors use anatomy like a map.

The skeleton gives shape, protects soft organs and gives muscles something to pull on. The skull protects the brain, the ribs protect the heart and lungs, and the spine protects the spinal cord. An adult has 206 bones. Babies have more because some bones join together as they grow.
Muscles attach to bones by tendons. When a muscle shortens it pulls a bone and the joint moves. Bones meet at joints, held by tough bands called ligaments.
Doctors use position words, such as upper and lower, front and back, so everyone knows the same place.

example.q: Which bones protect the heart and lungs, and what protects the brain?
steps: The heart and lungs sit in the chest.
The ribs form a cage around them.
The brain sits in the head, inside the skull.
example.a: Ribs protect the heart and lungs; the skull protects the brain

analogies.home: A house has a frame to hold it up. The skeleton is the body's frame.
analogies.city: Bridges have steel beams and cables. Bones are the beams and tendons are the cables.
analogies.sport: A rowing oar pivots on a rowlock. A bone pivots at a joint when a muscle pulls.
analogies.tech: A robot arm has rods and motors. Bones are the rods, muscles are the motors.

stages.mnemonic: Skull guards the brain, ribs guard the chest, spine guards the cord: top to bottom protection.
terms: The study of the structure of the body.
A strong cord joining muscle to bone.
A strong band joining bone to bone at a joint.
The framework of bones that supports and protects the body.

misc.right: Bones are living tissue. They have blood vessels, can heal after a break and make blood cells in their marrow.

trip.prompt: Find the skull, ribs and spine. Which bones do you think protect important organs?

questions.why: Bony structures guard soft, important organs.

questions.model: The skeleton supports the body and gives it shape, protects soft organs such as the brain and heart, and lets us move because muscles pull on bones.

panel.q: Why is it better that the brain is in a hard skull rather than in soft skin only?
panel.model: The brain is soft and easily injured, so a hard skull protects it from knocks.

teach.model: The skeleton is the body's frame. Bones support and protect organs, such as the skull for the brain. Muscles pull on bones through tendons, so joints move.

stages.title: Human physiology fundamentals
stages.hook: Your temperature stays near 37 °C whether it is a hot day or a cold night. How does your body keep it steady?
explain: Physiology is how the body works. Anatomy tells us what parts there are; physiology tells us what they do.
The body likes to keep conditions steady, such as temperature, water and blood sugar. This is called homeostasis. It works by sensing a change and then correcting it, like a thermostat in a house.
When you are hot, you sweat and blood vessels in the skin widen to lose heat. When you are cold, you shiver and blood vessels narrow to keep heat in. Normal body temperature is about 36.5 to 37.5 °C.

example.q: After running on a hot day, Tariq's skin is red and sweaty. Why?
steps: Running makes heat.
Body temperature starts to rise.
Skin blood vessels widen and sweat evaporates to cool him down.
example.a: His body is losing extra heat to keep temperature steady

analogies.home: A thermostat turns heating on and off to keep a room steady, like the body.
analogies.nature: A lizard moves between sun and shade. Our body has built-in controls.
analogies.tech: A car's cruise control keeps speed steady by correcting changes.
analogies.farm: A farmer opens vents in a greenhouse when it is too hot and closes them when cold.

stages.mnemonic: Sense, signal, fix: the body's thermostat loop.
terms: The study of how the body works.
Keeping conditions inside the body steady.
Salty water from the skin that cools you as it evaporates.
Rapid muscle shaking that makes heat.

misc.wrong: A fever means the thermostat is broken.
misc.right: In a fever the body deliberately sets a higher temperature to help fight infection. It still needs watching.

stages.limits: Normal values vary a little between people, the time of day and how temperature is measured. Patients here are fictional, and this is not medical advice.

stages.title: Cells and tissues
stages.hook: Your body is built from trillions of tiny units too small to see. What are they, and how do they group up?
explain: The cell is the basic unit of life. Your body has many kinds of cells, such as muscle cells, nerve cells and red blood cells. Each has a shape that suits its job.
Most cells have a nucleus that holds instructions (DNA), a membrane that is a skin around the cell, and mitochondria that release energy from food and oxygen.

Similar cells grouped together make a tissue. Four main tissue types are epithelial (coverings and linings), connective (supporting), muscle and nervous. Tissues group into organs, and organs into systems.

example.q: Put these in order from smallest to biggest: organ, cell, tissue, system.
steps: Cells are the smallest unit.
Similar cells form a tissue.
Tissues form an organ, and organs form a system.

analogies.home: Bricks make walls, walls make rooms, rooms make a house. Cells make tissues, tissues make organs.
analogies.city: People form teams, teams form departments, departments form a city service.
analogies.music: Notes make phrases, phrases make a tune. Cells make tissues and organs.
analogies.tech: Pixels make an image. Cells make the body.

stages.mnemonic: Cell, Tissue, Organ, System: C-T-O-S, small to big.
terms: The part of the cell that holds the DNA instructions.
A group of similar cells doing the same job.
The parts of a cell that release energy.

misc.wrong: All cells in the body look the same.
misc.right: Cells differ a lot. A nerve cell is long and branched, and a red blood cell is a small disc that carries oxygen.

stages.title: Body systems
stages.hook: When you stand up quickly, many parts react at once: your heart, nerves, muscles and blood vessels. How do they cooperate?
explain: A body system is a group of organs that work together. The circulatory system moves blood. The respiratory system moves air in and out. The digestive system breaks down food. The nervous system carries signals. The skeletal and muscular systems support and move us.
The urinary system filters blood and removes waste in urine. The endocrine system uses hormones, chemical messengers in the blood. The immune system defends against germs.
Systems depend on each other. Lungs bring in oxygen, but the circulatory system carries it. The nervous system controls how fast you breathe. A problem in one system can affect others.

example.q: Which two systems work together to get oxygen to your muscles?
steps: Oxygen enters through the lungs, part of the respiratory system.
Blood carries oxygen round the body.
Blood is moved by the circulatory system.

analogies.city: A city has roads, water pipes and electricity. Body systems keep the body running in the same way.
analogies.home: A home has plumbing, wiring and a kitchen. Each does a job but they depend on each other.
analogies.sea: A ship has an engine room, a bridge and cargo. Systems work together to keep it sailing.
analogies.sport: A team has attackers and defenders. Body systems cooperate to win health.

stages.mnemonic: Think of a city: roads (blood vessels), post (nerves), kitchen (digestive), police (immune).

stages.title: Nutrition and metabolism
stages.hook: A sleeping person still uses energy. Where does the body spend it, and where does it come from?
explain: Nutrition is how food supports the body. Food gives energy and the materials to grow and repair. The main nutrients are carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water. Fibre helps digestion.

Carbohydrates, such as rice, bread or maize, are the main quick fuel. Proteins, in beans, fish, eggs and meat, build and repair tissues. Fats store energy and are needed for some vitamins. Small amounts of vitamins and minerals are needed for many jobs: iron helps make red blood cells and calcium builds bones.

Metabolism is all the chemical reactions in the body that release and use energy. Even at rest the body uses energy for the heart, breathing, brain and keeping warm. Energy is measured in kilojoules or kilocalories.

example.q: Which nutrient mainly builds and repairs muscle?
steps: Muscle is made mostly of protein and water.
Foods such as beans, fish and eggs supply protein.
So protein builds and repairs.

analogies.farm: A farm needs seeds, tools and fuel. The body needs building materials (protein), fuel (carbohydrate) and helpers (vitamins).
analogies.city: A city needs fuel and building supplies. Food supplies both.
analogies.home: A house uses electricity even when nobody is awake. Your body uses energy at rest.
analogies.tech: A phone battery drains even when idle, like resting metabolism.

stages.mnemonic: Carbs for fuel, protein for repair, fats for store, vitamins and minerals for the small jobs.
terms: A substance in food that the body needs.
A nutrient that is the body's main quick fuel.
A nutrient that builds and repairs tissues.

misc.wrong: Fat in food is always bad.
misc.right: The body needs some fat for energy storage and to absorb some vitamins. Too much, especially over time, can harm health.

stages.limits: Needs vary with age, size, activity and health. A dietitian or doctor advises real people; this is general learning only. Patients here are fictional, and this is not medical advice.

stages.title: Microorganisms and infections
stages.hook: A tiny thing you cannot see can cause a big illness, while another tiny thing helps make yoghurt. What kinds of microorganisms are there?
explain: Microorganisms are living things too small to see without a microscope. Main kinds are bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites. Most microorganisms are harmless or helpful, and only a few cause disease.

Bacteria are single cells that can multiply on their own. Viruses are much smaller, not cells, and need to get inside our cells to multiply. Fungi include yeasts and moulds. Parasites live on or in another living thing.

An infection happens when a harmful microorganism gets in and multiplies. Germs spread by air, touch, water, food and bites from insects. Antibiotics work on bacteria. They do not work on viruses, so they are not used for colds or flu.

example.q: A doctor says a child's cold is caused by a virus. Would an antibiotic help?
steps: Colds are caused by viruses.
Antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses.
So an antibiotic would not help the virus.
example.a: No, antibiotics do not work on viruses

analogies.farm: Some soil microbes help crops grow, while others cause plant disease. It is the same for people.
analogies.home: Yoghurt needs helpful bacteria, yet other bacteria spoil food left out.
analogies.nature: Mushrooms are fungi that break down dead leaves.
analogies.city: Clean water works and sewers stop microbes spreading in towns.

terms: A living thing too small to see without a microscope.
Single-celled microorganisms; some cause disease, many are helpful.
A tiny infectious particle that multiplies inside living cells.
A medicine that kills or stops bacteria; it does not work on viruses.

misc.right: Antibiotics treat bacterial infections only. Wrong use can make bacteria resistant to them.

stages.limits: This is a simple picture. Real infection care needs a clinician to decide the cause and the treatment. Patients here are fictional, and this is not medical advice.

stages.title: The immune system
stages.hook: You catch measles once, and then almost never again. How does your body remember an enemy?
explain: The immune system defends against germs. The first defences are barriers: skin, the sticky mucus in the nose, stomach acid and tears. These stop many germs getting in.

If germs get in, white blood cells attack them. Some swallow germs. Others make antibodies, which are proteins that fit a particular germ and mark it for destruction. Swelling, redness and warmth at a cut show the immune system at work.

After an infection, the body keeps memory cells so it can respond faster next time. Vaccines safely train the immune system without causing the full illness. When many people are protected, it is harder for the germ to spread, which also shields people who cannot be vaccinated.

example.q: Why does a vaccine help the body fight a germ later?
steps: A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless piece or weak form of the germ.
The body makes antibodies and memory cells.
If the real germ arrives, the response is faster.
example.a: It trains the immune system to respond quickly

analogies.city: A city has walls, guards and police with photos of known criminals. Barriers, white cells and memory cells work like that.
analogies.home: A house has locks, an alarm and a family who recognises strangers.
analogies.sport: A goalkeeper who has seen a striker's tricks saves faster next time, like memory cells.
analogies.nature: A thorny bush keeps animals out, like skin keeps germs out.

terms: The body's defence against germs and harmful invaders.
A blood cell that helps fight infection.
A protein that fits a particular germ and helps remove it.
A safe way to train the immune system against a disease.

misc.wrong: Vaccines give you the disease on purpose.
misc.right: Vaccines use harmless parts or weakened or inactive forms of germs, or instructions to make a harmless piece, so the body learns without the full illness.

stages.limits: Vaccines can cause mild short-lived effects such as a sore arm. Rare serious effects are watched closely, and a doctor advises each real person. Patients here are fictional, and this is not medical advice.

panel.q: Why is a fever sometimes useful during an infection?
panel.model: A raised temperature can slow some germs and helps immune cells work, so a moderate fever is part of the defence response.
panel.why: Fever is a regulated response, not just a failure.

teach.model: The immune system protects us from germs. Skin is a barrier and white blood cells attack germs that get in. Antibodies and memory cells help the body respond faster next time, which is how vaccines work.

points.ask: What happens if germs get in?

stages.title: Symptoms and signs
stages.hook: A patient says 'I feel dizzy', while the nurse measures a fast pulse. Which one is a symptom and which is a sign?
explain: A symptom is something a patient feels and describes, such as pain, nausea or tiredness. A sign is something a clinician can observe or measure, such as a rash, a fever on the thermometer or a fast pulse.
Good clinicians ask questions about each symptom: where, when it started, how bad, what makes it better or worse, and other things that came with it. These details narrow down the cause.

Some signs and symptoms are red flags: they suggest something serious that needs urgent help, such as chest pain, trouble breathing, confusion, a stiff neck with fever, or heavy bleeding. All patients here are fictional; real people with such signs should seek urgent help.

example.q: A patient reports a headache. The doctor finds a temperature of 39.2 °C. Which is the symptom and which is the sign?
steps: A headache is felt and reported by the patient.
A temperature is measured by the doctor.
So the headache is a symptom and the temperature a sign.
example.a: Headache is the symptom; the high temperature is the sign

analogies.home: A smoke alarm beeping is a sign; the smell you notice yourself is a symptom.
analogies.sea: A sailor feels the boat rocking (symptom); the instrument reads the wave height (sign).
analogies.tech: A user says the app is slow (symptom); the log shows high delay (sign).
analogies.farm: A farmer sees a cow stand apart (sign); a vet asks what has changed.

stages.mnemonic: Symptom = Said by the patient. Sign = Seen or measured by the clinician.
terms: Something the patient feels and reports.
Something a clinician can see or measure.
A warning feature that may point to a serious cause.
When and how a symptom began.

misc.wrong: One symptom always points to one disease.
misc.right: Many illnesses share symptoms, so clinicians combine symptoms, signs and tests.

stages.limits: This simulation teaches reasoning with fictional patients. It is not personal medical advice; real symptoms should be checked by a qualified clinician.

trip.prompt: Find examples of signs and symptoms and sort them into the two groups.

questions.q: What is a symptom?
o: Something the patient feels and reports
Something only a machine can detect and measure
A result from a blood test
A kind of medicine for pain
questions.why: Symptoms are the patient's experience.

questions.q: What is a sign?
o: Something a clinician can observe or measure
A feeling only the patient knows
A kind of medicine on a ward
questions.why: Signs are objective findings.

questions.q: Which is a symptom?
o: A rash seen by the doctor
A pulse measured by a nurse
questions.why: Nausea is felt and reported.

questions.q: Which is a sign?
o: A fast pulse measured at 120 beats a minute
I feel tired all the time
I feel sad and low today
I feel dizzy when I stand
questions.why: A measured pulse is a sign.

questions.q: Match each item to the word that describes it.
questions.why: Symptoms are felt and reported; signs are observed or measured.

questions.q: A fictional patient has trouble breathing. How should a junior doctor act?
o: Treat it as urgent and call for senior help
Wait a few days and see
Ask them to go home and rest
questions.why: Trouble breathing is a red flag.

questions.q: Why do doctors ask 'when did it start?'
questions.why: Sudden or slow onset points to different causes.

questions.q: Many different illnesses can cause a cough. What does this mean for diagnosis?
o: Doctors need more clues than one symptom
A cough always points to one single disease
A cough means there is no disease
No further clues are ever needed
questions.why: Symptoms overlap, so we combine clues.

questions.q: Name two questions a doctor might ask about a pain.
questions.model: Where is the pain, when did it start, how bad is it, and what makes it better or worse?
questions.why: These questions describe a symptom clearly.

questions.q: A fictional child has fever and a very stiff neck and is hard to wake. This is...
o: A red-flag picture needing urgent senior help
A sign that it is safe to wait
Only a case of simple tiredness
questions.why: These could signal a serious infection and need urgent care.

panel.q: A patient feels well but a routine blood pressure is high. What is that?
panel.why: Some conditions show signs before symptoms.

panel.q: Why is a patient's own description important even when tests are normal?
o: Symptoms can show problems that tests miss
Tests are always right, so symptoms add nothing
Patients are always right about the cause
Descriptions are not useful to doctors
panel.why: The patient's experience is real and informative.

panel.q: Why is it safer to treat a red flag seriously even if it often turns out to be minor?
panel.model: Missing a serious cause can cause great harm, so red flags are checked quickly and escalated even if most turn out to be minor.
panel.why: The cost of missing a dangerous cause is high.

teach.model: A symptom is something the patient feels and tells you, such as pain. A sign is something the clinician can see or measure, such as a fever. Red flags are warnings that need urgent help.

stages.title: Introduction to patient care and communication
stages.hook: Two doctors give the same advice. Patients follow one doctor's advice but not the other's. What did the first do differently?
explain: Good care begins with good communication. Introduce yourself, speak kindly and clearly, and listen without interrupting. Use plain words rather than jargon, and check the patient has understood.

Respect each person's privacy, culture, language and choices. Use an interpreter if needed. Tell the truth gently. Patients have the right to ask questions and to say yes or no to a plan after it is explained. This is called consent.
Care is teamwork. Clear handovers to colleagues, writing accurate notes and asking a senior when unsure keep patients safe. Washing hands before and after each patient protects everyone.

example.q: A doctor wants to explain a plan to a worried grandmother who speaks another language. What is a good approach?
steps: Use a trained interpreter, not a young child.
Use plain words and short sentences.
Ask her to say back what she understood and invite questions.
example.a: Use an interpreter, plain words and check understanding

analogies.home: A good host welcomes guests and checks they are comfortable.
analogies.sport: A coach explains the play and checks the team understood before the match.
analogies.music: A duet only works when both players listen to each other.
analogies.city: A good guide gives clear directions and checks you know the way.

stages.mnemonic: Hello, Hear, Help, Check: greet, listen, explain, check understanding.
terms: A patient's informed agreement to a test or treatment.
Keeping a patient's information and body respected and private.
Passing important information about a patient to the next team.
Understanding and caring about how someone feels.

misc.wrong: Doctors should use difficult medical words so patients trust them.
misc.right: Trust grows from clear, plain words, honesty and listening.

stages.limits: Practices around consent and family involvement vary by country, age and law. The principles of respect and honesty are shared everywhere. Patients here are fictional, and this is not medical advice.

trip.prompt: Find what a person must be told before they can give informed consent.

questions.q: What is a good first step with a new patient?
o: Introduce yourself and greet them kindly
Start tests at once without speaking to them
Look at your phone while they talk
Ask them to leave the room politely
questions.why: A greeting builds trust.

questions.q: Which language should a doctor use?
o: A secret code shared only between doctors
questions.why: Clear words help the patient understand.

questions.q: What is consent?
o: Informed agreement to a test or treatment
A kind of medicine for pain
A hospital rule about visiting hours for relatives
questions.why: The patient agrees after understanding.

questions.q: Why use a trained interpreter rather than a child relative?
o: It is more accurate and does not burden the child
It is always cheaper for the hospital
Interpreters work too slowly to be useful
questions.why: Accuracy, privacy and the child's welfare matter.

questions.q: A medical student does not know the answer to a patient's question. What is best?
o: Say they will find out and ask a senior
Guess confidently so they feel reassured
Change the subject to something else
questions.why: Honesty and asking help keep patients safe.

questions.q: Order a simple patient conversation.
questions.why: Good communication flows from greeting to checking.

questions.q: Match each skill to its purpose.
questions.why: Each skill protects the patient.

questions.q: A patient says no to a test after it is explained. What should the team do?
o: Respect their choice and keep talking about options
Do the test anyway for their own good
Ignore what they said and continue
questions.why: A capable adult can refuse after being informed.

questions.q: Why wash hands before and after each patient?
o: To stop germs spreading between people
To make hands wet and cool
Because of habit and tradition, not safety
To see how the soap smells
questions.why: Hand hygiene prevents infection spread.

questions.q: Why check that a patient has understood your explanation?
questions.model: Checking understanding makes sure the patient can follow the plan and make an informed choice, and it avoids mistakes.
questions.why: Being heard is not the same as being understood.

panel.q: A young doctor is told off by a patient for using jargon. What is the best response?
o: Apologise and explain again in plain words
Use even more jargon and speak faster
Blame the patient for not understanding
panel.why: Learning and respect improve care.

panel.q: At handover a nurse forgets to say that a patient is allergic to a medicine. Why is that dangerous?
o: The next team may give a harmful medicine
It is not dangerous at all
The patient will get faster and better treatment
Allergies are not real medical problems
panel.why: Incomplete handover is a common cause of errors.

panel.q: Why should patients be told the truth even when the news is hard?
panel.model: Honest information builds trust and lets patients make their own choices, and it can be shared gently and with support.
panel.why: Honesty and compassion go together.

teach.topic: How to talk with a patient well
teach.model: Greet the patient kindly, listen, and explain in plain words. Check they understood and respect their choices, privacy and culture. If you do not know, say so and ask a senior.

points.ask: What if I do not know?
